title: India's Men's Badminton Stars Fall in Malaysia Masters Opening Round
excerpt: Sen outclassed by 18-year-old Indonesian prodigy; Prannoy squanders five match points in heartbreaking three-game loss to Japan's Naraoka
body:
The Malaysia Masters Super 500 in Kuala Lumpur was supposed to offer India's top male shuttlers a chance to reclaim momentum after a difficult Thomas Cup campaign. Instead, Wednesday's opening round delivered a double blow that has fans and pundits questioning whether Indian men's badminton is in a genuine crisis of confidence.

### A Teenager's Masterclass Against Sen

Lakshya Sen, seeded eighth and riding the high of reaching the All England Open final in March, was expected to cruise through the early rounds in Kuala Lumpur. Instead, he was comprehensively dismantled by Moh Zaki Ubaidillah — an 18-year-old Indonesian with two junior world medals to his name but precious little senior tour pedigree.

The scoreline tells the story: 17-21, 11-21 in just 43 minutes. Sen competed in the first game but was reduced to a spectator in the second, as Zaki's deceptive net play and relentless attacking instinct overwhelmed a player ranked 30 spots above him. For the Paris 2024 Olympic semifinalist, it was one of the most lopsided defeats of a season that has oscillated wildly between brilliance and bewilderment.

### Prannoy's Five Match Points That Vanished

If Sen's loss was surprising, HS Prannoy's was genuinely painful. The 33-year-old, defending champion of the 2023 edition of this very tournament, pushed World No. 9 Kodai Naraoka to the absolute limit. After dropping the first game 17-21 and clawing back the second 22-20, Prannoy held a commanding 20-16 lead in the decider — five match points in hand.

What followed was a collapse of almost unprecedented proportions. Naraoka reeled off eight of the last ten points to steal the match 22-24. It was the sort of finish that haunts a competitor's sleep: a victory that was practically signed, sealed, and then snatched away through a combination of the Japanese shuttler's courage and Prannoy's inability to execute at the death.

### The Women Carry India's Flag

While the men's campaign crumbled, India's women stepped up. Malvika Bansod, who has spent months recovering from an ACL injury, delivered a gutsy three-game victory over Germany's Yvonne Li, prevailing 21-17, 16-21, 21-9. Ashmita Chaliha also advanced, ensuring India maintains a presence in the later rounds.

The contrast is sharp. With PV Sindhu having withdrawn and the elite men's doubles pair of Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty opting out after their Thailand Open final run, India's 26-member squad was always going to lean heavily on Sen and Prannoy. Both delivered their worst possible performances on the same day.

### The Bigger Picture for Indian Badminton

This is not an isolated incident. India's 0-3 Thomas Cup semifinal loss to France earlier this month — without an injured Sen — exposed the thinness of the men's bench. Kiran George and Tharun Mannepalli, the next tier of Indian men's singles players, lack the experience and ranking points to consistently trouble the top 15. The Badminton Association of India (BAI) faces hard questions about talent development beyond the two headliners.

### What This Means for NRI Fans Abroad

For the growing community of Indian badminton fans in the diaspora — many of whom stayed up to watch the All England final on JioHotstar and BWF TV — the Malaysia Masters exit is a particular disappointment. Badminton has emerged as one of the sports where NRIs feel a genuine cultural connection, partly because of Prakash Padukone's pioneering legacy and partly because of the accessibility of BWF streaming globally.

The 2028 Los Angeles Olympics qualification window is now open, and ranking points from Super 500 events like Malaysia Masters carry real weight. Early exits mean lost points, which could have cascading effects on seedings at the Paris-level events that determine Olympic berths. For the thousands of diaspora fans who have organized watch parties and badminton leagues from Houston to Birmingham, the hope is that this week's stumble is a detour, not a trend.

### What's Next

The Malaysia Masters continues through Sunday, with India's remaining hopes pinned on Bansod, Chaliha, and the men's doubles pair of MR Arjun and Hariharan Amsakarunan, who pulled off a first-round upset of the seventh seeds. Sen and Prannoy will regroup for the Indonesia Open in June — another Super 500 event where they cannot afford another early departure if their Olympic ambitions are to remain on track.
